name: Classic Mac adventure games
title: Classic Mac Adventure Games and Infocom Text Adventures
description: Infocom text adventures and 1980s Macintosh adventure games, running in your browser: Hitchhiker's Guide, Deadline, Borrowed Time, King of Chicago and more.
keywords: infocom games online, text adventure online, hitchhiker's guide to the galaxy game, classic mac adventure games, interactive fiction, deadline infocom, 80s adventure games
body:
The Macintosh arrived in 1984 at the height of the text adventure, and for a few years adventure games were a large part of what there was to do on one. This page collects the ones that still run here: the Infocom catalogue, the illustrated parser games that tried to take Infocom on, and a handful of stranger experiments that did not fit either description.

Infocom, and why it was on the Mac from day one

Infocom did not write its games for any particular computer. It wrote them for the Z-machine, an imaginary computer of its own design, and then wrote a small interpreter for each real machine. Porting a catalogue to a new platform meant writing one interpreter, which is why Infocom titles were on the Macintosh almost as soon as the Macintosh was on sale. They boot here from original Infocom floppies, the same way they did then.

What is here covers most of the company's range. The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, written by Douglas Adams with Steve Meretzky, is the famous one and deserves to be: it is funny, and it is also unfair to the player on purpose, in ways that are part of the joke. Deadline was Infocom's first mystery, sold in a police dossier with interview transcripts and lab reports, and gives you twelve hours of game time to solve a murder. The Witness and Suspect followed it. Wishbringer was written as the introduction for newcomers and is the right one to start with. Seastalker was aimed at younger players. Infidel makes you play someone thoroughly unpleasant and then holds you to it. Cutthroats is a shipwreck-diving caper among people you should not trust.

The parser games with pictures

The Macintosh had a screen that could show pictures and a mouse, and a number of publishers bet that adventure games should use both. The most interesting of them came from a young Interplay, published by Activision. Mindshadow starts you on a beach with no memory. Borrowed Time is hard-boiled detective fiction in which you are the target of the murder. Tass Times in Tonetown is a surreal, punkish town that makes more sense once you stop expecting it to. All three keep a text parser and put a picture above it, and the later two add verbs you can click — an early Macintosh answer to how an adventure game should look.

Around them sit The Crimson Crown, Penguin Software's sequel to Transylvania; Dragonworld, adapted from a fantasy novel; and Star Trek: The Kobayashi Alternative, which gives you the Enterprise and a missing ship and leaves the rest to you.

The ones that fit no category

Hacker gives you a login prompt and nothing else — no manual, no objective, no hint of what the game is — and the discovery of what you are supposed to be doing is the game. Alter Ego is a life simulation told as a branching sequence of choices from birth onwards. The King of Chicago is one of Cinemaware's interactive films, and asks you to choose what your character thinks rather than what he does. Murder by the Dozen is twelve self-contained cases, closer to a puzzle book than to a story.

Playing them now

Text adventures run on the smallest machine here, a Macintosh Plus, and start in about a second. You will want a real keyboard: typing is the whole interface. Save often: the emulated machine keeps its disk between visits on titles that support it, but a parser game will still happily let you walk into a situation there is no way out of, and the only cure is an earlier save.

If you have never played one, the conventions are few. Type short commands — look, take lamp, north, examine desk. Abbreviations work: n for north, i for inventory, l to look again. The game understands far fewer words than English has, and part of the skill is learning which ones. When stuck, examine everything twice.

name: Classic Mac role-playing games
title: Classic Mac RPGs — Wizardry, Realmz, Cythera and More
description: Macintosh role-playing games from Wizardry and Rogue in 1985 to Realmz and Cythera in the shareware years, running in your browser with nothing to install.
keywords: classic mac rpg, mac role playing games, wizardry mac, realmz, cythera, rogue online, old computer rpg, dungeon crawler online
body:
The Macintosh was never the role-playing machine. The big series of the 1980s were written for the Apple II and the PC first, and some never came to the Mac at all. What did arrive, though, was often better suited to a mouse than the original, and the Mac grew a small, stubborn RPG culture of its own that peaked in the shareware years of the 1990s. Everything on this page runs in your browser.

Where the genre comes from

Wizardry: Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord is the source of the party-based dungeon crawl. Six characters, a marching order, a ten-level maze drawn in wireframe from the front of the party, and no automap. When a party dies down there the bodies stay until another party goes to fetch them. The Macintosh version replaced the Apple II's keyboard menus with windows and a mouse, and is one of the better ways to play the original. Wizardry II: The Knight of Diamonds was the first scenario disk anyone made for a computer RPG, and assumes you are bringing a party that has already finished the first game.

Rogue is the other root, and the one whose name became a genre. A dungeon generated anew every game, a single character, and death that is final. The version here is the 1985 Macintosh release, where A.I. Design threw away the letters and drew everything. Temple of Apshai Trilogy is older still in origin — the first Apshai, from 1979, is one of the earliest commercial computer RPGs — and this 1985 Macintosh rebuild gathers it and both sequels onto one disk.

Written for the Macintosh

A few RPGs of the 1980s were built for the Mac rather than ported to it, and you can tell. OrbQuest opens on an illuminated scroll and uses the Mac's windows the way the Mac's own software did. Legends of the Lost Realm came from Avalon Hill, the board wargame publisher, and plays with the density and the patience you would expect from that background. Neither is gentle for the first hour, and both repay the effort.

The shareware years

By the mid-1990s the most interesting Macintosh RPGs were being made by individuals and sold on the honour system. Realmz is the landmark: a turn-based party RPG in the Wizardry line, with a deep rule set and, more importantly, an engine that separated the game from its adventures, so that players wrote and swapped scenarios of their own for years. Cythera, published by Ambrosia, went the other way — an open island full of people with their own business, a plot you can miss entirely, and a world that does not organise itself around you. It is the one Mac RPG people still argue about.

Both are the unregistered shareware releases, distributed exactly as their authors distributed them. The registration notices are part of the software and are left in place, which is also what their licences ask for. See the shareware page for why that matters here.

Playing them now

These are long games. The good news is that titles here keep their disks between visits where they can, so a party rolled today is still there tomorrow — close the tab, come back, and the machine is where you left it. Save inside the game as well, because an emulated Macintosh is still a Macintosh and nothing stops a dungeon from killing everyone.

Expect to read. None of these games explain themselves the way modern ones do, and most assumed you had a manual open beside the keyboard. The individual pages carry the controls and the first steps; the rest is mapping on paper, which is still how these are best played.

name: Classic Mac board and card games
title: Classic Mac Board and Card Games — Chess, Solitaire, Shanghai
description: Chess, checkers, backgammon, Stratego, Shanghai and three solitaire collections from the classic Macintosh, playable in your browser with nothing to install.
keywords: classic mac solitaire, mac chess game, shanghai mahjong original, old mac card games, chessmaster 2000 online, stratego computer game, backgammon mac
body:
Board and card games were among the first things anybody wrote for the Macintosh, for an obvious reason: the machine could draw a chessboard or a playing card that looked like the real object, at a time when most computers could not. That was a genuine selling point in 1984, and the games on this page are the record of it — from a backgammon program written in the Mac's first months to the elaborate solitaire collections of the late 1990s.

Chess and its relations

Sargon III comes from Dan and Kathe Spracklen, whose original Sargon won the first microcomputer chess tournament in 1978. The Chessmaster 2000 is the program that turned chess software into a consumer product, on the strength of presentation as much as playing strength. Both are real opponents at their higher levels, on an eight-megahertz machine with one megabyte of memory.

Archon looks like chess and is not: when two pieces meet, the board gives way to an arena and they fight it out in real time. Stratego is Accolade's version of the board game of hidden ranks, and Pensate is a pure puzzle on a board — no randomness, no reaction time, a set of pieces that each move by a fixed rule, and a solution that is always there if you can see it.

The first-year software

Some of the most charming things here are the simplest. MacGammon! is backgammon with the doubling cube, copyright 1984. MacCheckers and Reversi puts both games in one application that fits on a 400K floppy with room to spare. MacMatch is a memory game from the same year and one of the oldest pieces of third-party Macintosh software that still runs. None of them are deep. All of them show what a small, well-made Macintosh program looked like before anyone had settled what one should look like.

Shanghai

Shanghai is the game most people know as mahjong solitaire, and this is the original commercial release. Brodie Lockard first wrote the idea on the PLATO system years earlier; Activision's 1986 Macintosh version is where it reached a wide audience, and the tile set drawn in one-bit black and white is still one of the handsomest things on the platform. Clear the pairs of free tiles until the heap is gone — or, more often, until it is not.

Solitaire, three ways

By the late 1990s solitaire on the Mac was its own small industry. Solitaire Till Dawn was the collection Mac owners actually had: dozens of variants on one engine, with rules for each and statistics kept per game. Hardwood Solitaire II bet on looks — a rendered wooden table and cards that looked like objects. Absolute Solitaire came in a box from MacSoft. All three are the shareware or demo releases, left exactly as they were distributed, limits and registration notices included.

Playing them now

The 1984–86 titles boot on an emulated Macintosh Plus in about a second and are comfortable on a phone. The solitaire collections run on Mac OS 8.6 and take longer to start, since they are booting a whole later Macintosh rather than a floppy. Most of these games are played entirely with the mouse, which makes them among the easiest things on the site to simply pick up.

name: Classic Mac action and arcade games
title: Classic Mac Arcade Games — Dark Castle, Maelstrom, Crystal Quest
description: Macintosh action and arcade games from Dark Castle and Crystal Quest to Maelstrom and Glider PRO, playable in your browser with nothing to download.
keywords: classic mac arcade games, dark castle online, maelstrom mac, crystal quest, glider pro online, old mac action games, mac shooter games, 90s mac games
body:
The Macintosh was sold as a serious machine, and for its first few years Apple did very little to encourage anyone to think otherwise. The action games that appeared on it anyway were made by small teams who liked the hardware — its sharp screen, its mouse, its sound — and built things that could not have been made the same way anywhere else. Many of them are still among the best-looking games of their decade. Everything below runs in a browser tab.

The black-and-white years

Dark Castle is the one people remember. A platformer from Silicon Beach Software with digitised sound, drawn in pure black and white, controlled with the keyboard and the mouse together, and notoriously hard. Its programmer, Jonathan Gay, went on to create the software that became Flash. Beyond Dark Castle is the sequel and every bit as unforgiving. Lode Runner is the Macintosh version of the classic dig-and-collect puzzle-platformer, Mouse Stampede is one of the very few pure arcade score-chasers the machine got in 1985, and Skyfox put a flight combat game on a nine-inch monochrome screen.

Colour arrives

When the Macintosh II brought colour in 1987, Crystal Quest was one of the first games to use it: fly around a single screen collecting crystals, avoid everything else, reach the exit. It is simple, very fast, and has a sound design people still quote. Crystal Crazy is its stranger sequel. Shufflepuck Café is air hockey in an alien bar against a cast of opponents with real personalities, and Prince of Persia is Jordan Mechner's rotoscoped platformer in its Macintosh release.

The shareware golden age

The early 1990s is where Mac action games found their own voice, mostly through shareware. Maelstrom took Asteroids and gave it rendered rocks, a real soundtrack and screen-shaking weight; it is still one of the best arcade games on any Macintosh. Arashi did the same for Tempest. Glypha is Joust in an Egyptian tomb, and Glider PRO, from the same author, is a paper aeroplane riding air vents through a house full of hazards — gentle, clever, and open source today. Later there is Avara, Mighty Mike, Ferazel's Wand and Space Debris, and a long tail of smaller games made by one or two people in their spare time.

Sport and speed

The action category here also holds the sports games: One on One, Dr. J against Larry Bird; Earl Weaver Baseball, which modelled real managerial strategy; Sierra Championship Boxing; and The Duel: Test Drive II, a Ferrari against a Porsche on a road full of other people's lanes.

Playing them now

Action games are the demanding end of emulation, and most of these run at the speed they were meant to on any recent laptop. Use a keyboard where a game asks for one; phones work for the mouse-driven titles and struggle with the rest. Several of the colour games ask to switch the monitor to 256 colours when they start — say yes, which is what they expect. Each title's page lists its controls, and the controls sheet on the player shows them again while you play.

name: Classic Mac shareware games
title: Classic Mac Shareware Games — Ambrosia, Pangea and the Archives
description: The Macintosh shareware scene of the 1990s, playable in your browser: Maelstrom, Realmz, Cythera, Mighty Mike and dozens more, distributed as their authors allowed.
keywords: mac shareware games, ambrosia software games, classic mac shareware, 90s mac games, info-mac archive, tucows mac games, maelstrom, realmz, pangea software
body:
For about fifteen years the most interesting games on the Macintosh were not sold in shops. They were uploaded to archives, copied onto magazine cover discs, passed around on floppies, and paid for — sometimes — by people who mailed a cheque to an address in a Readme file. This page collects the Macintosh shareware that runs here, and it is the part of the catalogue this site can host with the clearest conscience, because most of it was written to be copied.

How shareware worked

The deal was simple and entirely on trust. You could have the program free, try it, give copies to friends and put it on a bulletin board. If you kept using it, you were asked to pay the author, and in return you usually got a registration code that removed a reminder screen or unlocked the later levels. Distribution was the author's marketing, which is why so many shareware licences explicitly allow anyone to redistribute the unregistered version, as long as nothing is changed and nobody charges for it.

That is the licence this site relies on, and it is followed literally. Every title here is the unregistered release, complete and unmodified. The reminder screens are left exactly where their authors put them — you will meet several of them — and nothing has been patched to remove a limit. Each title's page says where its copy came from and what its licence says, and the reasoning is set out in what shareware licences actually say.

Ambrosia

Ambrosia Software was the best-known name in Mac shareware and the most polished. Maelstrom came first and is still the best argument that an arcade game could be made better by rethinking it rather than copying it. Avara was a networked 3D combat game in 1996, Barrack an action-puzzle game, Ferazel's Wand a platformer with some of the best sprite art of the period, and Cythera the most ambitious thing Ambrosia ever published: an open-world role-playing game on an island. Ambrosia's reminder screens were famous in their own right, and they are all here.

The individuals

Much of the best shareware was one person's work. John Calhoun's Glypha was freeware from the author of Glider. Brian Greenstone's Mighty Mike, released by his own Pangea Software, is the game MacPlay later sold as Power Pete. Tim Phillips built Realmz and kept it going for most of a decade. Peter N. Lewis, better known for the internet software he wrote, made Greebles. Space Debris is one of many games Richard Bannister put out. Arashi was released by its authors as freely distributable along with the tools they built to make it.

There is also a long tail of smaller work that shows what the scene was actually like: Sapiens, from two brothers in Toulouse, which opens by asking whether you would like it in English or French; Star Fighters, written in Future BASIC; Spins!, whose splash screen advertises a web address that no longer goes anywhere; and solitaire, breakout and arcade games from people whose names are known now only from their own title screens.

Where they came from

The copies here come from the same places they always did: the big archives — Info-Mac, the University of Michigan's Mac archive, and later Tucows — preserved and mirrored long after the originals went offline. Many of the authors are still reachable, and some of their companies still exist. If you wrote something on this page and would rather it were not here, the takedown page explains how to ask, and it will come down.

Playing them now

Most of the late-1990s shareware runs on Mac OS 8.6, which means booting a whole later Macintosh, so these take a little longer to start than the floppy-era games. Expect a registration reminder before most of them; the page for each game says which button lets you play on. Registering is, alas, no longer possible for most of these, which is a strange kind of freedom the authors never intended to give.
